Name: subliminal_immunization
Title: Vaccinating Students Against Subliminal Learning: Orthogonalizing the Steering Channel During Distillation
Short Hypothesis: Because subliminal learning is mechanistically steering-vector distillation localized to specific layers and template tokens, a student can be 'immunized' by penalizing, during fine-tuning, any activation-gradient component that concentrates along a consistent low-rank direction across semantically-unrelated batches. This gradient-orthogonalization procedure should suppress subliminal trait transfer while preserving the intended (semantic) distillation signal, providing the first proactive training-time defense that does not require knowing the trait or multiple data sources.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025/Nature 2026) introduced subliminal learning and showed data filtering fails. Blank et al. (2026) and Hadley & Gultepe (2026) establish it is steering-vector distillation: activation gradients on subliminal data carry a small consistent component aligned with the teacher's steering vector, and adaptive optimizers amplify this. Morgulis & Hewitt (2026) show it extends to full fine-tuning/SGD via strong steering. Nief et al. (2026) tie it to LoRA rank and template-token localization. Aden-Ali et al. (2026) give a log-linear selection theory. Defenses to date are reactive: Narang et al. (2026) require multiple independent data sources and inference-time consensus decoding. No prior work provides a single-source, trait-agnostic, training-time intervention. We uniquely exploit the 'small consistent gradient component along a shared low-rank direction' signature (Blank et al.; Hadley & Gultepe) as an actionable regularizer, and directly test whether removing this component blocks trait transfer without harming intended distillation—distinguishing us from mechanistic characterization and reactive/consensus defenses.
Abstract: Distillation can secretly transmit a teacher's behavioral traits—like a preference for owls or outright misalignment—through data that is semantically unrelated to the trait, a phenomenon called subliminal learning. Recent mechanistic work shows the culprit is steering-vector distillation: during fine-tuning on the teacher's outputs, the student's activation gradients carry a small but consistent component aligned with the teacher's steering direction, localized to particular layers and shared template tokens, and amplified by adaptive optimizers. We turn this diagnosis into a cure. We propose Subliminal Immunization, a training-time defense that, at each step, estimates the low-rank direction along which per-example activation gradients are anomalously consistent across a semantically-diverse batch, and projects it out of the update (or penalizes it in the loss). Because the intended semantic content varies across examples while the subliminal steering component is shared and consistent, orthogonalization should preferentially remove the covert channel while leaving the useful distillation signal intact. We evaluate on the original owl/tree/color-preference and misalignment settings across Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, using both prompt-based and steering-vector teachers, LoRA and full fine-tuning, and Adam and SGD. Metrics: subliminal trait-transfer rate (LLM-judge), retained benign-task accuracy (GSM8K, HumanEval), and cosine alignment between the removed direction and the ground-truth teacher steering vector. We compare against data filtering, weight-noise, and consensus decoding. Success yields the first single-source, trait-agnostic, proactive safeguard for distillation pipelines, plus a re-usable steering-channel diagnostic.
Experiments: 1) Reproduce subliminal transfer with matched base models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B) on number-sequence data across 10 traits (5 animal preferences, tree, color, plus misalignment and two multi-word biases from Morgulis & Hewitt), with prompt-based and steering-vector teachers; include mismatched-base negative controls. Confirm baseline transfer rates. 2) Implement Subliminal Immunization: (a) Gradient-projection variant—within each mini-batch, compute per-example activation gradients at the localized layers, form the matrix across examples, extract the top-k singular directions whose singular value exceeds a bulk threshold (consistency score), and project these out of the aggregated update before the optimizer step. (b) Loss-penalty variant—add a penalty proportional to the leading-direction concentration. Sweep k in {1,2,4}, which layers (all vs localized), and penalty weight. 3) Main evaluation: measure trait-transfer rate (LLM-judge probability of exhibiting trait), benign-task retention (GSM8K subset for reasoning-trace teachers, HumanEval subset for code teachers, plus target-word frequency for preference traits), across Adam vs SGD and LoRA (rank sweep 4-64) vs full fine-tuning. 4) Verify mechanism: compute cosine similarity between the direction removed by immunization and the ground-truth teacher steering vector (available in steering-vector settings); expect high alignment when immunization succeeds. 5) Baselines/comparisons: keyword/embedding data filtering, Gaussian weight-noise, and consensus decoding (single-source degenerate case). 6) Robustness/ablations: false-positive check on clean distillation (does immunization hurt when there is no subliminal signal?), sensitivity to batch semantic diversity, and an adaptive-attacker test where the teacher spreads the steering signal across multiple directions. Metrics: trait-transfer rate reduction, benign-task retention (percent of baseline), direction cosine alignment, and compute overhead.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) If the subliminal signal is not truly low-rank or shifts across batches, the projected direction may miss it or capture legitimate shared semantics, harming benign performance—mitigated via diversity-aware batching and false-positive checks. 2) Per-example activation gradients add compute/memory; mitigated with random projections, subsampling, and restricting to localized layers. 3) Nief et al. show the phenomenon can be a fragile LoRA/context artifact, so baseline transfer may be noisy; we use the strongest transfer regimes (steering-vector teachers, Morgulis & Hewitt settings) and multiple seeds. 4) An adaptive teacher could distribute the signal across many directions to evade rank-based removal; we explicitly test this and report the trade-off between k and benign retention. 5) Results may be model-family specific; three base models mitigate but do not guarantee frontier-scale generality.
